credit.label: homestead credit
credit.note: Arkansas taxes a home on 20% of its market value. Every homestead gets up to a $600 credit off the bill (Amendment 79); the state repays the local governments for it, so they still receive the full amount shown below.
credit.limits: The $600 homestead credit is applied in full when the bill is large enough; Amendment 79 also limits how fast a homestead’s assessed value can rise, which isn’t modeled.

split_note: Each government’s share is split by the mills it levies: the school district’s operating mills versus its bond (debt) mills, as the state lists them. City and county taxes are one slice each; the county’s spending is on the money trail.
rollback_note: Florida and Texas publish a yearly “no-raise” rate. Arkansas doesn’t: its rates are set in mills, and after a countywide reassessment Amendment 59 rolls millage back so the reassessment alone doesn’t raise more money. School millage changes need a vote of the district’s voters at the school election — so the biggest lever on most Arkansas bills is a school election that usually draws far fewer voters than November.
hearing: County and city millage is levied by the quorum court and city council each fall; school millage is set by the district’s voters at the school election.
limits: Rates are from the state’s 2025 Millage Report (2026 collections), page 79.
County and city taxes are shown as single slices; the county’s own spending is on the money trail.
